catalog_quote: Looking, firstly, at monomorphemic Nouns, pitch seems to be the clearest correlate of acoustic prominence. In bisyllabic Nouns of a variety of syllabic structures, in the overwhelming majority of cases the second syllable is more prominent than the first. Of 47 investigated tokens in isolation (and thus presumably in their citation form), the second syllable has higher pitch at the midpoint of the vowel than the first in 40 cases. ... In trisyllabic, monomorphemic Nouns too, pitch seems to be the most reliable determinant of acoustic prominence. Across 33 word tokens of a wide range of syllabic structures, only two pitch patterns were found: 24 tokens showed highest pitch on the last syllable, somewhat lower pitch on the first syllable, and much lower pitch on the second syllable ... audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held Van Gysel 2024 PDF/txt at the stated pages (151, 153-157). Deciding source is the best available: a 2024 dissertation-grammar by the language's main documenter with Praat measurements; no later or more specialised prosody study exists in Glottolog or Crossref. The one competing grammar-length work (Silva Gomes 2013, UNICAMP) was downloaded from the open UNICAMP repository and read: it has no stress section but states (fn.32 p.96; pp.128-129) that stress falls preferentially on the word-final syllable, is the Sanapaná default, and is 'defined locally, not by syllable type' — independently confirming our right-edge/final coding and the no-weight note.
